business_rule: The application config is a dictionary subclass that can be read and modified like any dict.
Certain config values are forwarded to the Flask object so they can be read and written as app attributes (e.g. app.testing).
Multiple config keys can be set at once using the dict update method.
Flask and its extensions store their own settings in the same config object as the application's settings.
Debug mode should be enabled with the --debug option on the flask command rather than in config or code.
Setting DEBUG in code is discouraged because flask run cannot read it early and extensions may already have configured themselves.
When debug mode is on, flask run uses the interactive debugger and the reloader by default.
The DEBUG value is set from the FLASK_DEBUG environment variable and maps to the app.debug attribute.
DEBUG defaults to False.
Debug mode must not be enabled in a production deployment.
When TESTING is enabled, exceptions propagate instead of being handled by the app's error handlers.
When TESTING is enabled, extensions may change their behavior to make testing easier.
TESTING defaults to False and should be enabled in your own tests.
When PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS is true, exceptions are re-raised rather than handled by the app's error handlers.
When PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS is unset, it is implicitly true if TESTING or DEBUG is enabled.
When TRAP_HTTP_EXCEPTIONS is enabled and no handler exists for an HTTPException, the exception is re-raised to the interactive debugger instead of returned as an error response.
TRAP_HTTP_EXCEPTIONS defaults to False.
Accessing a missing key in request dicts such as args or form returns a 400 Bad Request by default.
When TRAP_BAD_REQUEST_ERRORS is enabled, a missing request key is treated as an unhandled exception so the interactive debugger is shown.
When TRAP_BAD_REQUEST_ERRORS is unset, it is enabled in debug mode.
The SECRET_KEY is used to securely sign the session cookie and may be used by extensions for other security needs.
The SECRET_KEY should be a long random bytes or str value.
The SECRET_KEY must never be revealed in public posts or committed code.
SECRET_KEY defaults to None.
SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS holds old secret keys that can still be used to unsign data, allowing key rotation without invalidating active sessions.
The default implementation tests the last fallback key in the list first, so keys should be ordered oldest to newest.
Fallback keys should be removed after an appropriate period because each additional key adds checking overhead.
Extensions that use SECRET_KEY may not yet support SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS.
The session cookie name defaults to 'session' and can be changed to avoid clashing with an existing cookie.
When SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN is not set, browsers send the session cookie only to the exact domain that set it.
When SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN is set, browsers send the session cookie to that domain and all its subdomains.
Leaving SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN unset is more restrictive and more secure than setting it.
Changing SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN after browsers already hold a cookie may create a second cookie that is sent in undefined order.
SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN does not fall back to SERVER_NAME.
When SESSION_COOKIE_PATH is not set, the session cookie is valid under APPLICATION_ROOT, or under '/' if that is not set.
Session cookies are marked HTTP-only by default so browser JavaScript cannot access them.
When SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is enabled, browsers send the session cookie only over HTTPS.
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE defaults to False and only makes sense when the app is served over HTTPS.
When SESSION_COOKIE_PARTITIONED is enabled, browsers scope the cookie to the top-level document's domain to prevent third-party cookies leaking between sites.
Enabling SESSION_COOKIE_PARTITIONED implicitly enables SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE.
SESSION_COOKIE_PARTITIONED defaults to False and should be enabled for cookies expected to work in embedded third-party contexts.
SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE restricts cross-site cookie sending and accepts 'Lax' (recommended) or 'Strict'.
SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE defaults to None.
When session.permanent is true, the cookie expiration is set PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME seconds in the future.
PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME accepts either a timedelta or an integer number of seconds.
PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME defaults to 31 days (2678400 seconds).
The default cookie session rejects a signature older than PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME.
When SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST is true and the session is permanent, the cookie is sent with every response.
SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST defaults to True.
SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST does not affect non-permanent sessions.
When USE_X_SENDFILE is enabled, Flask sets the X-Sendfile header instead of serving file data itself.
USE_X_SENDFILE defaults to False and only makes sense with a web server that recognizes the header.
SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT sets the cache-control max age for served files as a timedelta or integer seconds.
The file cache max age can be overridden per file with get_send_file_max_age on the app or blueprint.
When SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT is None, browsers are told to use conditional requests instead of a timed cache.
When a request host does not match TRUSTED_HOSTS, a SecurityError is raised and a 400 error is returned.
When TRUSTED_HOSTS is None, all hosts are considered valid.
A TRUSTED_HOSTS entry matches exactly, or matches any subdomain when it starts with a dot.
Trusted host validation happens during routing, and before_request and after_request callbacks still run.
SERVER_NAME must be set when subdomain matching is enabled so the subdomain can be extracted from the request.
SERVER_NAME must be set for url_for to generate external URLs outside a request context.
SERVER_NAME does not restrict incoming requests to only that domain.
Setting SERVER_NAME does not implicitly enable subdomain matching.
SERVER_NAME does not affect SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN.
APPLICATION_ROOT tells the app which path it is mounted under for generating URLs outside a request context.
Inside a request, the dispatcher's SCRIPT_NAME is used instead of APPLICATION_ROOT.
APPLICATION_ROOT defaults to '/'.
PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME sets the scheme for external URLs generated outside a request context and defaults to 'http'.
When a request body exceeds MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH, a 413 RequestEntityTooLarge error is raised.
When MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH is None, no request size limit is enforced at the application level.
When MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH is None and the request has no Content-Length and the server does not signal stream termination, no data is read.
MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH can be overridden for a specific view via Request.max_content_length.
When a non-file field in a multipart form exceeds MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE bytes, a 413 RequestEntityTooLarge error is raised.
MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE defaults to 500000 bytes, and None disables the limit.
MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE can be overridden for a specific view via Request.max_form_memory_parts.
When a multipart form contains more fields than MAX_FORM_PARTS, a 413 RequestEntityTooLarge error is raised.
MAX_FORM_PARTS defaults to 1000, and None disables the limit.
MAX_FORM_PARTS can be overridden for a specific view via Request.max_form_parts.
When TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD is enabled, templates are reloaded when their files change.
When TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD is unset, it is enabled in debug mode.
When EXPLAIN_TEMPLATE_LOADING is enabled, Flask logs how each template file was located and loaded.
EXPLAIN_TEMPLATE_LOADING defaults to False.
A warning is issued when cookie headers exceed MAX_COOKIE_SIZE, which defaults to 4093 bytes.
Setting MAX_COOKIE_SIZE to 0 disables the oversized cookie warning.
Setting PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS to False disables automatically generated OPTIONS responses app-wide.
PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS can be overridden per route via the provide_automatic_options attribute.
PRESERVE_CONTEXT_ON_EXCEPTION was removed in Flask 2.2.
ENV was removed in Flask 2.3.
The JSON_* and JSONIFY_* config keys were removed in Flask 2.3 in favor of attributes on the app.json provider.
LOGGER_NAME and LOGGER_HANDLER_POLICY were removed in Flask 1.0.
Configuration can be loaded from a module or object with from_object.
Configuration can be loaded from a file whose path is held in an environment variable with from_envvar.
Values loaded later override values loaded earlier, so defaults are loaded first and deployment settings second.
Only uppercase names in a configuration file are stored in the config object.
Configuration should be loaded very early so extensions can access it at startup.
Configuration can be loaded from any file format with from_file by passing a load function.
Loaders that read binary files, such as tomllib.load, require text=False.
from_prefixed_env loads every environment variable starting with a prefix into the config.
The from_prefixed_env prefix defaults to FLASK_ and can be changed with the prefix argument.
The prefix is stripped from environment variable names to form the config key.
Environment values are parsed with json.loads by default, and the parser can be changed with the loads argument.
With the default JSON parsing, only lowercase 'true' and 'false' are valid boolean values.
A double underscore in an environment variable name sets a key in a nested dictionary.
Missing intermediate keys in a nested environment variable path are initialized as empty dicts.
On Windows, environment variable keys are always uppercase, so nested keys become uppercase.
Creating the app in a factory function allows multiple instances with different configurations for easier testing.
Code should not require configuration at import time so the app can be reconfigured later.
Configuration should be loaded before extensions call init_app.
A default configuration should be kept in version control and overridden by a separate deployment-specific configuration.
An environment variable should be used to switch between configurations without touching code.
Configurations can be organized as classes that inherit shared settings from a base config class.
from_object does not instantiate a config class, so it must be instantiated first to use properties.
Only uppercase property names on an instantiated config object are loaded as config values.
The instance folder is meant for deployment-specific files and runtime-changing data and is not meant to be under version control.
An explicitly provided instance_path must be an absolute path.
For an uninstalled module or package, the default instance folder is an 'instance' folder next to it.
For an installed module or package, the default instance folder is $PREFIX/var/<appname>-instance.
Relative config filenames resolve against the application root by default.
Setting instance_relative_config=True makes relative config filenames resolve against the instance folder.
from_pyfile with silent=True does not fail when the config file is missing.
open_instance_resource opens a file relative to the instance folder.
A signal notifies all of its subscribers by calling each one when the event it represents occurs.
Flask signals are implemented with the Blinker library.
Extensions may provide their own signals in addition to Flask's built-in ones.
Unlike decorator-based handlers, signals can be subscribed to temporarily.
Unlike decorator-based handlers, signal subscribers cannot directly affect the application.
A function subscribes to a signal with connect and can optionally specify a sender to listen to.
A function unsubscribes from a signal with disconnect.
For all core Flask signals, the sender is the application that issued the signal.
Subscribers should specify a sender unless they intend to listen to signals from all applications.
Subscriber functions should accept **extra so they do not break if Flask adds new signal arguments.
connected_to temporarily subscribes a function for the duration of a with block.
The connect_via decorator subscribes the decorated function to a signal for a given sender.
Custom signals should be created as named signals in a Blinker Namespace.
A signal's name makes it unique and is available through its name attribute.
A signal is emitted with send, which takes a sender first and forwards keyword arguments to subscribers.
A class emitting a signal should pass self as the sender.
A plain function emitting a signal should pass current_app._get_current_object() as the sender.
The current_app proxy must never be passed directly as a signal sender.
Context-local proxies such as g are available to subscribers between request_started and request_finished.
A blueprint is not an application but a recorded set of operations that are executed when registered on an application.
Blueprints share the application's config, unlike separate applications dispatched at the WSGI layer.
A blueprint cannot be unregistered without destroying the whole application object.
A blueprint does not need to define view functions and can provide only templates, static files, filters, or other utilities.
A blueprint's route decorator records the view so it is registered when the blueprint is registered on an app.
A blueprint's endpoints are prefixed with the blueprint name and a dot.
A blueprint's name changes its endpoints but not its URLs.
A blueprint registered with url_prefix has all its routes mounted under that prefix.
Parameters in a blueprint's URL prefix or subdomain become common view arguments for all its views.
A blueprint can be registered multiple times on one app with different URL rules.
Whether a blueprint works correctly when registered multiple times depends on its implementation.
A blueprint can be registered on another blueprint.
A nested blueprint's name is prefixed with its parent's name.
A nested blueprint's URLs are prefixed with its parent's URL prefix.
A nested blueprint's subdomain is prefixed onto its parent's subdomain.
Request hooks such as before_request registered on a parent blueprint also run for its child blueprints.
If a child blueprint has no handler for an exception, the parent blueprint's error handler is tried.
A blueprint's resource folder is the package named by its import name, or the containing package if it is a module.
A blueprint's root_path attribute shows its resource folder.
open_resource opens a file relative to the blueprint's resource folder.
A blueprint exposes static files from static_folder, given as an absolute path or relative to the blueprint's location.
A blueprint's static files are served at its url_prefix plus the folder name by default, changeable with static_url_path.
A blueprint's static endpoint is named <blueprint_name>.static.
A blueprint without a url_prefix cannot serve its static folder because the app's /static route takes precedence.
Blueprint static folders are not searched as a fallback when a file is missing from the app's static folder.
A blueprint's template_folder is added to the template search path at lower priority than the app's template folder.
An application template overrides a blueprint template with the same relative path.
When multiple blueprints provide the same template path, the first registered blueprint takes precedence.
Blueprint templates should be placed in a subfolder named after the blueprint to avoid being accidentally overridden.
url_for builds URLs for blueprint endpoints using the blueprint name and a dot as a prefix.
Within a blueprint view or template, an endpoint starting with only a dot refers to an endpoint in the same blueprint.
Blueprints support the errorhandler decorator for blueprint-specific error pages.
Blueprint 404 and 405 handlers are only invoked by raise or abort inside the blueprint's views, not by invalid URLs.
Handling 404 or 405 differently by URL prefix must be done in an app-level handler that inspects request.path.
The request proxy is only available when a request context is active.
Sessions can only be used when the app's secret key is set.
Sessions are stored in a signed cookie that the user can read but cannot modify without the secret key.
The secret key should be complex and unguessable.
The session proxy is only available when a request context is active.
The session tracks assignment and access of keys but cannot detect changes to mutable values.
After mutating a list or dict in the session, session.modified must be set to True manually.
By default the browser clears the session cookie when it is closed.
Setting session.permanent to True persists the cookie for PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME.
The app.permanent_session_lifetime attribute is always a timedelta even if the config value is an integer.
The session implementation can be replaced by providing a custom session interface.
The g object stores data valid for a single request or app context and is safe in threaded environments.
The g object is only available when an app context is active.
The g object has been bound to the application context instead of the request context since Flask 0.10.
The current_app proxy is only available when an app context is active.
Flask uses Python's built-in json module by default.
The JSON implementation can be changed by setting json_provider_class or app.json.
flask.json functions use the app's JSON provider methods when an app context is active.
The Jinja tojson filter uses the app's JSON provider and marks its output as safe.
RequestContext is deprecated since Flask 3.2, merged into AppContext, and will be removed in Flask 4.0.
request_ctx is deprecated since Flask 3.2, merged into app_ctx, and will be removed in Flask 4.0.
template_rendered is sent after a template is successfully rendered, with the template and context.
before_render_template is sent before template rendering begins, with the template and context.
request_started is sent after the request context is set up and before any request processing happens.
request_finished is sent right before the response is sent to the client, with the response.
got_request_exception is sent when an unhandled exception occurs during request processing, including in debug mode.
got_request_exception is not sent for HTTPExceptions or exceptions with registered handlers unless raised from an error handler.
request_tearing_down is always sent when the request tears down, even if an exception occurred.
request_tearing_down subscribers currently run after regular teardown handlers, but this order is not guaranteed.
request_tearing_down passes the causing exception, if any, as the exc keyword argument.
appcontext_tearing_down is always sent when the app context tears down, even if an exception occurred.
appcontext_tearing_down passes the causing exception, if any, as the exc keyword argument.
appcontext_pushed is sent with the application as sender when an application context is pushed.
appcontext_popped is sent with the application as sender when an application context is popped.
message_flashed is sent when the app flashes a message, with the message and its category.
A URL rule can be registered with the route decorator, with add_url_rule, or directly on url_map.
Variable parts of a URL rule are written in angle brackets and passed to the view as keyword arguments.
By default a URL variable accepts any text without a slash.
The int converter accepts integers and the float converter accepts floating point values.
The path converter accepts text including slashes.
The any converter matches one of a provided set of items.
The uuid converter accepts UUID strings.
Custom URL converters can be defined through url_map.
If a rule ends with a slash and is requested without one, the user is redirected to the URL with the slash.
If a rule has no trailing slash and is requested with one, a 404 Not Found is raised.
Multiple URL rules can point to the same view function, but each rule must be unique.
A URL rule can specify default values for its variables.
A URL that contains a rule's default value is redirected to the simpler URL with a 308 redirect.
A default route should only handle GET because redirects cannot preserve form data.
The endpoint defaults to the view function's name unless explicitly provided.
A view function can be attached to an endpoint later by storing it in view_functions.
A blueprint view's endpoint is always prefixed with the blueprint name, which the function cannot customize.
By default a URL rule listens only for GET and implicitly HEAD.
OPTIONS is implicitly added and handled for URL rules since Flask 0.6.
Allowed methods for a rule must be passed as keyword arguments.
If methods are not given when registering a rule, Flask uses the view function's methods attribute if it exists.
A view's provide_automatic_options attribute forces automatic OPTIONS handling on or off for that view.
Methods in a view's required_methods attribute are always added even if methods are overridden in route().
